questions.q: What is 'embedding' in MongoDB schema design?
options: Storing related data as a nested sub-document or array inside the parent document
Storing a document's _id inside a separate index collection
Compressing a document before writing it to disk
Replicating a document across multiple shards
questions.explain: Embedding nests the related data directly inside the parent document, rather than in a separate collection.

questions.q: What is the real performance and consistency case for embedding, per this lesson?
options: One query reads parent and child together, and a single-document write is atomic
It guarantees the document will never exceed 16MB
It removes the need for any indexes
It automatically distributes the data across shards
questions.explain: Embedding means a single find gets both pieces of data, and updating the embedded data is one atomic document write.

questions.q: How do you combine data from a referencing relationship (e.g. a post's authorId and the users collection) in a single query?
options: Using a `$lookup` aggregation pipeline stage, MongoDB's server-side join
MongoDB automatically embeds referenced documents at read time with no extra syntax
References cannot ever be combined in a single query
By adding a FOREIGN KEY constraint to the collection
questions.explain: `$lookup` is the aggregation stage that performs a server-side join across two collections in one query.

questions.q: What real constraint on embedding does this lesson identify?
options: A single BSON document has a hard 16MB size limit, so unbounded embedded arrays can hit that ceiling
Embedded documents cannot contain arrays
MongoDB limits embedding to exactly one level of nesting
Embedded fields cannot be indexed
questions.explain: The 16MB document size limit is real, and an ever-growing embedded array can approach or exceed it.

questions.q: Per this lesson's guidance, when does referencing fit better than embedding?
options: One-to-many or many-to-many relationships, large/unbounded data, or data that changes independently and often
Only when the two collections are on different physical servers
Only for one-to-one relationships
Never — embedding is always the better choice in MongoDB
questions.explain: Referencing suits data shared across many documents, unbounded growth, and data with its own independent update cadence.
